I am sixty-four years old, and I have worked these fields in Quzhou for forty years. My wife and I are the only labor left in our household, so I must plan for what our four hands can actually finish. Cotton is the backbone of my farm—this soil knows cotton, and the buyers know me. I will put 5.5 mu into hybrid Bt cotton this spring. I will run the rotary tiller across the field in late April, spread my base fertilizer, and sow when the ground warms. I will irrigate four times from our well: at planting if the spring is dry, at early flowering, at peak boll, and again in late August so the boils do not dry out before opening. I will split the nitrogen—part at sowing, more at flowering—and lay the phosphorus and potassium down at the base. Five pesticide sprays are enough now; the Bt cotton handles bollworm, but I still must watch for aphids and red spider mites. I expect 260 kg of seed cotton per mu; I do not trust the exaggerated numbers on seed bags.

The remaining 2 mu I keep in stevia. It is a perennial, so it will rise from the roots when the frost leaves. The leaf buyers pay decent money, but cutting and sun-drying the leaves is hard work for two old people, so I do not plant more. I will till between the rows in spring, give it moderate fertilizer, and irrigate five times because stevia leaves turn bitter if they go thirsty. I will spray only twice unless I see worms. I expect about 300 kg of dry leaves per mu, which is an honest return for the labor we can spare.
